claim: Transposable elements (TEs) comprise almost half of primate genomes.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) comprise almost half of primate genomes and their aberrant regulation can result in deleterious effects.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (Jurka, 2000; de Koning et al., 2011).

claim: Aberrant regulation of TEs can result in deleterious effects.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) comprise almost half of primate genomes and their aberrant regulation can result in deleterious effects.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific understanding of TE biology.

claim: In pluripotent stem cells, rapidly evolving KRAB-ZNF genes target TEs for silencing by H3K9me3.
source: In pluripotent stem cells, rapidly evolving KRAB-ZNF genes target TEs for silencing by H3K9me3.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2010; Najafabadi et al., 2015; Turelli et al., 2014; Friedli et al., 2014; Wolf and Goff, 2009; Schultz et al., 2002).

claim: H3K9me3 ChIP-seq experiments were performed in induced pluripotent stem cells from 10 human and 7 chimpanzee individuals.
source: To investigate the evolution of TE silencing, we performed H3K9me3 ChIP-seq experiments in induced pluripotent stem cells from 10 human and 7 chimpanzee individuals.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: Four million orthologous TEs were identified between humans and chimpanzees.
source: We identified four million orthologous TEs and found the SVA and ERV families to be marked most frequently by H3K9me3.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's analysis.

claim: The SVA and ERV families are marked most frequently by H3K9me3.
source: We identified four million orthologous TEs and found the SVA and ERV families to be marked most frequently by H3K9me3.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: As many as 82% of putatively silenced TEs are marked at similar levels in humans and chimpanzees.
source: We found little evidence of inter-species differences in TE silencing, with as many as 82% of putatively silenced TEs marked at similar levels in humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis of H3K9me3 enrichment.

claim: TEs that are preferentially silenced in one species are a similar age to those silenced in both species.
source: TEs that are preferentially silenced in one species are a similar age to those silenced in both species and are not more likely to be associated with expression divergence of nearby orthologous genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TE sequence divergence from consensus sequences.

claim: TEs preferentially silenced in one species are not more likely to be associated with expression divergence of nearby orthologous genes.
source: TEs that are preferentially silenced in one species are a similar age to those silenced in both species and are not more likely to be associated with expression divergence of nearby orthologous genes.
evidence: This is based on the integrated analysis of H3K9me3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: There is limited species-specificity of TE silencing across 6 million years of primate evolution.
source: Our data suggest limited species-specificity of TE silencing across 6 million years of primate evolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the overall data analysis.

claim: Over half of primate genomes are annotated as transposable elements.
source: Over half of primate genomes are annotated as transposable elements (TEs) (Jurka, 2000; de Koning et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to RepeatMasker annotations and previous studies.

claim: Many of the same TEs are present in both human and chimpanzee species.
source: Considering the degree of sequence similarity between the human and chimpanzee genomes, it is not surprising that many of the same TEs are present in both species (Chimpanzee Sequencing and Analysis Consortium, 2005; Ramsay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing studies.

claim: TE activity, especially from endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), has declined in the hominid lineage relative to other mammalian lineages.
source: In general, TE activity, especially from endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), has declined in the hominid lineage relative to other mammalian lineages (Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the human genome project paper.

claim: A fraction of evolutionarily recent TEs are active in the human genome, including HERV-K ERVs.
source: However, a fraction of evolutionarily recent TEs are active in the human genome, including HERV-K ERVs (Tönjes et al., 1996; Medstrand and Mager, 1998; Fuchs et al., 2013; Klawitter et al., 2016; Wildschutte et al., 2016), members of the Alu (Batzer and Deininger, 1991; Batzer et al., 1991), L1 (Kazazian et al., 1988, Brouha et al., 2003), and SVA (Wang et al., 2005; Ostertag et al., 2003) families.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on active TEs.

claim: Members of the Alu, L1, and SVA families are active in the human genome.
source: However, a fraction of evolutionarily recent TEs are active in the human genome, including HERV-K ERVs (Tönjes et al., 1996; Medstrand and Mager, 1998; Fuchs et al., 2013; Klawitter et al., 2016; Wildschutte et al., 2016), members of the Alu (Batzer and Deininger, 1991; Batzer et al., 1991), L1 (Kazazian et al., 1988, Brouha et al., 2003), and SVA (Wang et al., 2005; Ostertag et al., 2003) families.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on active TEs.

claim: TEs are considered a potential source of regulatory innovation.
source: Because of their transposition competence, TEs are considered a potential source of regulatory innovation (Kazazian, 2004; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on TE function.

claim: TEs can serve as primate-specific regulatory sequence.
source: Indeed, TEs can serve as primate-specific regulatory sequence (Jacques et al., 2013; Trizzino et al., 2017), act as enhancer elements (Lynch et al., 2011; Chuong et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2013), carry transcription factor binding sites (Wang et al., 2007; Bourque et al., 2008; Kunarso et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012), and contribute themselves to the transcriptome (Faulkner et al., 2009; Kelley and Rinn, 2012; Kapusta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating regulatory functions of TEs.

claim: TEs can act as enhancer elements.
source: Indeed, TEs can serve as primate-specific regulatory sequence (Jacques et al., 2013; Trizzino et al., 2017), act as enhancer elements (Lynch et al., 2011; Chuong et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2013), carry transcription factor binding sites (Wang et al., 2007; Bourque et al., 2008; Kunarso et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012), and contribute themselves to the transcriptome (Faulkner et al., 2009; Kelley and Rinn, 2012; Kapusta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TE-derived enhancers.

claim: TEs can carry transcription factor binding sites.
source: Indeed, TEs can serve as primate-specific regulatory sequence (Jacques et al., 2013; Trizzino et al., 2017), act as enhancer elements (Lynch et al., 2011; Chuong et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2013), carry transcription factor binding sites (Wang et al., 2007; Bourque et al., 2008; Kunarso et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012), and contribute themselves to the transcriptome (Faulkner et al., 2009; Kelley and Rinn, 2012; Kapusta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on transcription factor binding to TEs.

claim: TEs contribute to the transcriptome.
source: Indeed, TEs can serve as primate-specific regulatory sequence (Jacques et al., 2013; Trizzino et al., 2017), act as enhancer elements (Lynch et al., 2011; Chuong et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2013), carry transcription factor binding sites (Wang et al., 2007; Bourque et al., 2008; Kunarso et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012), and contribute themselves to the transcriptome (Faulkner et al., 2009; Kelley and Rinn, 2012; Kapusta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TE transcription.

claim: Human-specific TEs become aberrantly activated (marked by H3K4me3) on human chromosome 21 in the mouse cellular environment.
source: However, human-specific TEs become aberrantly activated (marked by H3K4me3) on human chromosome 21 in the mouse cellular environment (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Host repressive factors needed to properly silence human TEs may be absent in the mouse nuclear environment.
source: It was therefore speculated that host repressive factors needed to properly silence these human TEs may be absent in the mouse nuclear environment, which is ~60 million years diverged from human.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of aberrant TE activation in the mouse environment.

claim: The observation of aberrant TE activation in mouse cells suggests a relatively rapid evolution of TE silencing mechanisms.
source: This suggested a relatively rapid evolution of TE silencing mechanisms, in line with the evolutionary arms race hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous observation.

claim: In embryonic stem cells (ESCs), KRAB-ZNFs can recognize TEs in a sequence-specific manner.
source: In particular, it has been shown that in embryonic stem cells (ESCs), KRAB-containing Zinc Finger genes (KRAB-ZNFs) can recognize TEs in a sequence-specific manner, recruit the co-factor TRIM28 (also known as KAP1), and histone methyltransferase SETDB1 (also known as ESET), to effect silencing through the deposition of the repressive histone three lysine nine trimethylation (H3K9me3) modification (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2010; Najafabadi et al., 2015; Turelli et al., 2014; Friedli et al., 2014; Wolf and Goff, 2009; Schultz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on KRAB-ZNF-mediated TE silencing.

claim: KRAB-ZNFs recruit the co-factor TRIM28 and histone methyltransferase SETDB1 to effect silencing through H3K9me3 deposition.
source: In particular, it has been shown that in embryonic stem cells (ESCs), KRAB-containing Zinc Finger genes (KRAB-ZNFs) can recognize TEs in a sequence-specific manner, recruit the co-factor TRIM28 (also known as KAP1), and histone methyltransferase SETDB1 (also known as ESET), to effect silencing through the deposition of the repressive histone three lysine nine trimethylation (H3K9me3) modification (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2010; Najafabadi et al., 2015; Turelli et al., 2014; Friedli et al., 2014; Wolf and Goff, 2009; Schultz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on the KRAB-ZNF silencing pathway.

claim: After the establishment of TE silencing by H3K9me3, TEs are subjected to de novo DNA methylation.
source: After the establishment of TE silencing by H3K9me3, TEs are subjected to de novo DNA methylation, which persists in somatic and germ cells (Rowe and Trono, 2011; Quenneville et al., 2012; Rowe et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2014; Karimi et al., 2011; Walter et al., 2016; Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Barau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on DNA methylation of TEs.

claim: DNA methylation of TEs persists in somatic and germ cells.
source: After the establishment of TE silencing by H3K9me3, TEs are subjected to de novo DNA methylation, which persists in somatic and germ cells (Rowe and Trono, 2011; Quenneville et al., 2012; Rowe et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2014; Karimi et al., 2011; Walter et al., 2016; Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Barau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on DNA methylation maintenance.

claim: Some TEs can evade detection by host KRAB-ZNFs by acquiring mutations.
source: Some TEs can evade detection by host KRAB-ZNFs by acquiring mutations.
evidence: This is based on the understanding of the evolutionary arms race between TEs and host silencing mechanisms.

claim: Host repressor mechanisms need to evolve rapidly in order to maintain genome integrity.
source: It was thus hypothesized that the host repressor mechanisms need to evolve rapidly in order to maintain genome integrity (Kapopoulou et al., 2016; Huntley et al., 2006; Thomas and Schneider, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TEs are silenced by KRAB-ZNFs particularly in early embryonic development.
source: TEs are silenced by KRAB-ZNFs particularly in early embryonic development (Chuong et al., 2017), their most likely niche for retrotransposition (Richardson et al., 2017); however, it is difficult to obtain biological material from humans and other primates to determine how this process evolves.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TE silencing in development.

claim: Early embryonic development is the most likely niche for retrotransposition.
source: TEs are silenced by KRAB-ZNFs particularly in early embryonic development (Chuong et al., 2017), their most likely niche for retrotransposition (Richardson et al., 2017); however, it is difficult to obtain biological material from humans and other primates to determine how this process evolves.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on TE activity in development.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) provide a model of the cells of the embryonic inner cell mass.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) provide a model of the cells of the embryonic inner cell mass to sidestep this challenge.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about iPSC biology.

claim: HERVH elements are not silenced but actively transcribed and functionally relevant in human iPSCs.
source: This cell type is of further interest as we know of examples of primate-specific TEs that are not silenced, but actively transcribed and functionally relevant in this cell type in human (notably HERVH elements) (Klawitter et al., 2016; Santoni et al., 2012; Fort et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Grow et al., 2015; Wissing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on HERVH expression in pluripotent cells.

claim: The activity of HERVH elements in iPSCs might imply specificity of TE regulatory mechanisms.
source: This might imply specificity of TE regulatory mechanisms, and hints at the fact that evolutionarily recent TE sequence could play a role in differentiating gene regulatory networks between species.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of HERVH activity.

claim: Evolutionarily recent TE sequence could play a role in differentiating gene regulatory networks between species.
source: This might imply specificity of TE regulatory mechanisms, and hints at the fact that evolutionarily recent TE sequence could play a role in differentiating gene regulatory networks between species.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of HERVH activity.

claim: A panel of non-retroviral reprogrammed iPSCs from multiple humans and chimpanzees has been established.
source: The establishment of a panel of non-retroviral reprogrammed iPSCs from multiple humans and chimpanzees has allowed us to comprehensively characterize the extent of TE silencing in both species (Gallego Romero et al., 2015; Banovich et al., 20162018; Burrows et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies establishing these cell lines.

claim: H3K9me3 is the predominant output of KRAB-ZNF-targeted silencing mechanisms in pluripotent cells.
source: In order to gain insight into how TE regulation, specifically TE silencing, evolves between humans and chimpanzees, we globally profiled the predominant output of KRAB-ZNF-targeted silencing mechanisms in pluripotent cells: the histone modification H3K9me3.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the KRAB-ZNF silencing pathway.

claim: Differences in TE silencing do not drive substantial gene regulatory divergence between humans and chimpanzees in iPSCs.
source: Our observations led us to conclude that, at least in our comparative iPSC system, differences in TE silencing do not drive substantial gene regulatory divergence between these two closely related species.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the integrated analysis of H3K9me3 and gene expression data.

claim: All iPSC lines used in the study were confirmed to have a normal karyotype.
source: Briefly, all cell lines were confirmed to have a normal karyotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), have the ability to form embryoid bodies that consist of cells from the three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), display global gene expression signatures consistent with pluripotent cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and express key pluripotency factors detectable by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All iPSC lines have the ability to form embryoid bodies that consist of cells from the three germ layers.
source: Briefly, all cell lines were confirmed to have a normal karyotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), have the ability to form embryoid bodies that consist of cells from the three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), display global gene expression signatures consistent with pluripotent cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and express key pluripotency factors detectable by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All iPSC lines display global gene expression signatures consistent with pluripotent cells.
source: Briefly, all cell lines were confirmed to have a normal karyotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), have the ability to form embryoid bodies that consist of cells from the three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), display global gene expression signatures consistent with pluripotent cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and express key pluripotency factors detectable by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All iPSC lines express key pluripotency factors detectable by immunocytochemistry.
source: Briefly, all cell lines were confirmed to have a normal karyotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), have the ability to form embryoid bodies that consist of cells from the three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), display global gene expression signatures consistent with pluripotent cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and express key pluripotency factors detectable by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: All samples were processed in species-balanced batches at each experimental step.
source: All samples were processed in species-balanced batches at each experimental step (Table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design to control for batch effects.

claim: Data from different individuals cluster by species.
source: As expected, data from different individuals cluster by species (with the exception of one human individual, which therefore was removed from subsequent analysis; Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10), and inter-species variation in read counts is somewhat greater than intra-species variation (Spearman's correlation in human vs. human = 0.90, chimpanzee vs. chimpanzee = 0.89, and human vs. chimpanzee = 0.80, Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10.

claim: Inter-species variation in H3K9me3 read counts is somewhat greater than intra-species variation.
source: As expected, data from different individuals cluster by species (with the exception of one human individual, which therefore was removed from subsequent analysis; Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10), and inter-species variation in read counts is somewhat greater than intra-species variation (Spearman's correlation in human vs. human = 0.90, chimpanzee vs. chimpanzee = 0.89, and human vs. chimpanzee = 0.80, Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: At FDR < 0.01, 16,288 (11%) regions were classified as differentially enriched between the two species.
source: At FDR < 0.01, we classified 16,288 (11%) regions as differentially enriched between the two species (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 12 and see examples in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis using DESeq2.

claim: The proportion of differentially enriched regions is robust with respect to data filtering choices.
source: The proportion of differentially enriched regions is robust with respect to our data filtering choices (Figure 1—figure supplement 13 and Table 4 in Supplementary file 1), and the choice of approach to analyze the data (Table 5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 13 and Tables 4-5.

claim: 80.2% of all annotated human TEs are orthologous between humans and chimpanzees.
source: To compare TE silencing by H3K9me3 across species, we identified a comprehensive set of 4,036,865 autosomal orthologous TEs in the human and chimpanzee genomes (80.2% of all annotated human TEs, see Materials and methods and Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the orthologous TE identification pipeline.

claim: 12% of orthologous TEs (436,049 instances) overlap an orthologous H3K9me3 region with at least 50% of their length.
source: We considered the ChIP-seq data in the context of the orthologous TEs, and observed that 12% of orthologous TEs (436,049 instances) overlap an orthologous H3K9me3 region with at least 50% of their length (denoted 'overlapping', Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3; we note that our subsequent conclusions are robust with respect to the specific cutoff used to classify a TE as overlapping with H3K9me3 regions).
evidence: This is a direct result from overlapping TEs with H3K9me3 regions.

claim: There is enrichment of LTRs among TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Turelli et al., 2014; Karimi et al., 2011), we found enrichment of LTRs (Pearson's Chi-squared test; p<0.001), and SVA elements (p<0.001), among TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: There is enrichment of SVA elements among TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Turelli et al., 2014; Karimi et al., 2011), we found enrichment of LTRs (Pearson's Chi-squared test; p<0.001), and SVA elements (p<0.001), among TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: TEs that are silenced in both species are located further away from the TSS than TEs that are silenced preferentially in one species.
source: We next considered proximity of TEs to genes by determining the distance between each TE and the closest orthologous annotated Transcription Start Site (TSS). TEs that are silenced in both species are significantly further away from the TSS than TEs that are preferentially silenced in one species, or those that do not overlap with H3K9me3 regions (p<0.001; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TEs that show greater divergence in silencing across species are more likely to be closer to the TSS than TEs with lower divergence.
source: TEs that show greater divergence in silencing across species are also more likely to be closer to the TSS than TEs with lower divergence (p<0.001; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Gene expression levels decrease when TEs in the cis-regulatory window overlap with H3K9me3 regions.
source: As expected, we observed that gene expression levels decrease when TEs in the cis-regulatory window overlap with H3K9me3 regions (p<0.01; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 79% of windows containing at least one orthologous H3K9me3 region overlapping a TE have similar levels of H3K9me3 enrichment in human and chimpanzee.
source: Of the windows that contain at least one orthologous H3K9me3 region overlapping a TE, 79% have similar levels of H3K9me3 enrichment in human and chimpanzee (3,523), with 11% of regions enriched in human (499), and 10% of regions enriched in chimpanzee (463), at FDR of 1% (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis of H3K9me3 in gene regulatory windows.

claim: There is no significant difference in expression divergence effect size between genes associated with species-specific or shared TE silencing using 10, 20 or 40 kb windows upstream of the TSS.
source: We found no significant difference in the expression divergence effect size between genes associated with species-specific or shared TE silencing, using 10, 20 or 40 kb windows upstream of the TSS (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a weak, negative association between gene expression and silencing divergence when considering silenced TEs located within 1 kb upstream of the TSS.
source: We did find a weak, negative association between gene expression and silencing divergence when we considered silenced TEs that are located within 1 kb upstream of the TSS (only 165 genes in that set; Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4; Table 7 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: H3K9me3 enrichment in regions that overlap a 1 kb region around the TSS is associated with expression divergence, irrespective of the presence of a TE.
source: It is tempting to conclude that TEs (or silenced TEs) near the TSS can have a marked contribution to expression divergence; however, H3K9me3 enrichment in regions that overlap a 1 kb region around the TSS is similarly associated with expression divergence, irrespective of the presence of a TE (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genes that are classified as differentially expressed between humans and chimpanzees are not more likely to be associated with inter-species differences in H3K9me3 at TEs in their putative regulatory regions.
source: We found no association between silencing and inter-species expression divergence: genes that are classified as differentially expressed between humans and chimpanzees are not more likely to be associated with inter-species differences in H3K9me3 at TEs in their putative regulatory regions (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The correlation between inter-species effect sizes for gene expression divergence and H3K9me3 enrichment is weak (Pearson's correlation = −0.0005 in a 10 kb window).
source: Indeed, when we considered the entire distribution, the correlation between inter-species effect sizes for gene expression divergence and H3K9me3 enrichment is weak (Pearson's correlation = −0.0005 in a 10 kb window; the correlation in divergence increases somewhat to −0.14 when considering a 1 kb window upstream of the TSS; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from correlation analysis.

claim: HERVH elements are expressed in human and chimpanzee iPSCs.
source: Indeed, we find HERVH to be expressed in human and chimpanzee iPSCs, and to be depleted for H3K9me3, suggesting that this element is essential for the pluripotency network in both humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: HERVH elements are depleted for H3K9me3 in iPSCs.
source: Indeed, we find HERVH to be expressed in human and chimpanzee iPSCs, and to be depleted for H3K9me3, suggesting that this element is essential for the pluripotency network in both humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is based on H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: HERVH elements are essential for the pluripotency network in both humans and chimpanzees.
source: Indeed, we find HERVH to be expressed in human and chimpanzee iPSCs, and to be depleted for H3K9me3, suggesting that this element is essential for the pluripotency network in both humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression and lack of silencing of HERVH elements.

claim: As many as 84% of genomic regions enriched for the active histone modification, H3K27ac, are similar between humans and chimpanzees in iPSC-derived neural crest cells.
source: For example, as many as 84% of genomic regions enriched for the active histone modification, H3K27ac, are similar between humans and chimpanzees in iPSC-derived neural crest cells (Prescott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The chromatin landscape is generally highly conserved in primates.
source: More broadly, while gene expression differences between primates have been shown to often be associated with inter-species differences in histone modifications (Cain et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014), the chromatin landscape is generally highly conserved in primates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and the current study's findings.

claim: The study provides further support for the notion that chromatin state is generally highly conserved between closely related primate species.
source: Our results provide further support for the notion that chromatin state is generally highly conserved between closely related primate species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: TEs have not substantially rewired pluripotent stem cell gene regulatory networks between humans and chimpanzees.
source: We have not found evidence that TEs, whether orthologous or not, have substantially rewired pluripotent stem cell gene regulatory networks between humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the integrated analysis of H3K9me3 and gene expression data.

claim: Longer TEs may be silenced more often because they are more likely to have unwanted regulatory potential.
source: Put together, these observations suggest that longer TEs may be silenced more often because they are more likely to have unwanted regulatory potential, and are therefore more likely to contain sequences that recruit silencing machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that longer TEs overlap H3K9me3 more often.

claim: Longer TEs are more likely to contain sequences that recruit silencing machinery.
source: Put together, these observations suggest that longer TEs may be silenced more often because they are more likely to have unwanted regulatory potential, and are therefore more likely to contain sequences that recruit silencing machinery. This is consistent with the finding that more KRAB-ZNF proteins (sequence-specific mediators of TE silencing) bind longer TEs (Imbeault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a study showing KRAB-ZNF binding to longer TEs.

claim: More KRAB-ZNF proteins bind longer TEs.
source: This is consistent with the finding that more KRAB-ZNF proteins (sequence-specific mediators of TE silencing) bind longer TEs (Imbeault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TEs that are silenced similarly in both species are evolutionarily less diverged from the consensus sequence than TEs that do not overlap H3K9me3 regions.
source: We found that TEs that are silenced similarly in both species are evolutionarily less diverged from the consensus sequence than TEs that do not overlap H3K9me3 regions (p<0.001; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When inter-species differences in silencing are larger, the sequences of the TEs are more diverged from the consensus sequence.
source: Across all TEs, we did not find a difference in sequence divergence between TEs that are silenced in just one or both species (Figure 5C) but stratification of TEs by the magnitude of the inter-species silencing effect reveals that when inter-species differences in silencing are larger, the sequences of the TEs are more diverged from the consensus sequence (p<0.001; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TEs preferentially silenced in human overlap annotated regulatory regions less frequently compared with TEs preferentially silenced in chimpanzee.
source: We found that TEs that are preferentially silenced in human overlap annotated regulatory regions less frequently compared with TEs that are preferentially silenced in chimpanzee (p<0.001; Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: TEs preferentially silenced in human overlap regions of active gene regulation less often than TEs preferentially silenced in chimpanzee.
source: We found that TEs that are preferentially silenced in human overlap regions of active gene regulation less often than TEs preferentially silenced in chimpanzee. The active chromatin annotations we considered include marking by H3K27ac, DHS, enhancer elements (marked by H3K4me1, p300) and regions marked by RNA polymerase II occupancy (for all comparisons p<0.01; Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: There is no significant difference between TEs preferentially silenced in either species with respect to overlap with the active promoter-associated mark, H3K4me3.
source: Notably, there is no significant difference between TEs preferentially silenced in either species with respect to overlap with the active promoter-associated mark, H3K4me3.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of overlap with H3K4me3 regions.

claim: The SVA and LINE TE classes show a reduction in the proportion of TEs overlapping H3K9me3 regions in the non-orthologous and species-specific categories.
source: However, within each species, the SVA and LINE TE classes show a reduction in the proportion of TEs overlapping H3K9me3 regions in the non-orthologous, and species-specific categories (p (SVA) <0.001; p (LINE) <0.001); Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 85% of orthologous SVA elements overlap H3K9me3, but only 41% of non-orthologous SVA elements overlap the regions marked by H3K9me3.
source: For example, 85% of orthologous SVA elements overlap H3K9me3, but only 41% of non-orthologous SVA elements overlap the regions marked by H3K9me3.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of SVA element overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: 17% and 14% orthologous and non-orthologous LINE elements overlap H3K9me3 regions, respectively.
source: In contrast, 17% and 14% orthologous and non-orthologous LINE elements overlap H3K9me3 regions, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of LINE element overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: There is a reduction of TE and H3K9me3 overlap in human LTRs.
source: We also found a reduction of TE and H3K9me3 overlap in human LTRs (p<0.001), but an increase in H3K9me3 overlap with LTRs that are chimpanzee-specific (p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an increase in H3K9me3 overlap with LTRs that are chimpanzee-specific.
source: We also found a reduction of TE and H3K9me3 overlap in human LTRs (p<0.001), but an increase in H3K9me3 overlap with LTRs that are chimpanzee-specific (p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: More recent TEs are generally less likely to be silenced.
source: In general, these observations are consistent with the notion that more recent TEs are generally less likely to be silenced, in line with the evolutionary arms race theory (Kapopoulou et al., 2016; Huntley et al., 2006; Thomas and Schneider, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that non-orthologous TEs are less likely to be silenced, supported by citations to the evolutionary arms race theory.

claim: When TEs do overlap H3K9me3 regions, they are generally (82% of TEs) silenced to the same extent in the two species.
source: Indeed, while ultimately most TEs (88%) do not overlap H3K9me3 regions, when TEs do overlap H3K9me3 regions, they are generally (82% of TEs) silenced to the same extent in the two species.
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparative analysis of H3K9me3 enrichment at TEs.

claim: Most TEs (88%) do not overlap H3K9me3 regions.
source: Indeed, while ultimately most TEs (88%) do not overlap H3K9me3 regions, when TEs do overlap H3K9me3 regions, they are generally (82% of TEs) silenced to the same extent in the two species.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of TE overlap with H3K9me3 regions.

claim: 53,201 TEs are enriched for H3K9me3 in human.
source: Our analysis includes hundreds of thousands of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions; thus even just 18% of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 and are silenced differently across species still comprise of tens of thousands of instances (53,201 TEs enriched for H3K9me3 in human, and 28,110 TEs in chimpanzee).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis.

claim: 28,110 TEs are enriched for H3K9me3 in chimpanzee.
source: Our analysis includes hundreds of thousands of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions; thus even just 18% of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 and are silenced differently across species still comprise of tens of thousands of instances (53,201 TEs enriched for H3K9me3 in human, and 28,110 TEs in chimpanzee).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis.

claim: Less than 20% of 2,079 orthologous HERVH elements overlap with H3K9me3 regions.
source: Notably, less than 20% of 2,079 orthologous HERVH elements, which are generally known to be expressed in pluripotent cells, overlap with H3K9me3 regions (compared to 80% of 3,484 THE1B elements, which are not known to be expressed in pluripotent cells, for example).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of HERVH element overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: 80% of 3,484 THE1B elements overlap with H3K9me3 regions.
source: Notably, less than 20% of 2,079 orthologous HERVH elements, which are generally known to be expressed in pluripotent cells, overlap with H3K9me3 regions (compared to 80% of 3,484 THE1B elements, which are not known to be expressed in pluripotent cells, for example).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of THE1B element overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: 82% of 21,710 L1 elements that overlap H3K9me3 are similarly silenced in both species.
source: However, of those L1 elements that overlap H3K9me3, the majority (82% of 21,710 elements) are similarly silenced in both species (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of L1 element silencing.

claim: TEs silenced in at least one species are longer than those that do not overlap orthologous H3K9me3 regions.
source: On average, TEs silenced in at least one species are longer than those that do not overlap orthologous H3K9me3 regions (Wilcoxon-rank sum test; p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Artificially longer TEs do not overlap with H3K9me3 regions more often, suggesting that TE elements are silenced in a non-random manner.
source: To confirm that longer TEs do not overlap H3K9me3 more often by chance alone, we artificially increased the length of the non-overlapping TEs to match the median length of TEs marked by H3K9me3 in both species. The artificially longer TEs do not overlap with H3K9me3 regions more often, suggesting that TE elements are silenced in a non-random manner, which cannot be simply explained by length in itself.
evidence: This is based on a control analysis to test whether length alone explains H3K9me3 overlap.

claim: Shorter TEs are associated with higher silencing divergence.
source: When we stratified TEs by the magnitude of inter-species silencing divergence (absolute effect size), we found that shorter TEs are associated with higher silencing divergence (p<0.001; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the proportion of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions and the median length of the TEs in the family (Pearson's correlation = 0.93).
source: Interestingly, across TE families there is a strong correlation between the proportion of TEs that overlap H3K9me3 regions and the median length of the TEs in the family (Pearson's correlation = 0.93; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a direct result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Within families the median length of TEs that do not overlap H3K9me3 is highly similar to that of TEs that do (Pearson correlation for median TE lengths across families = 0.99).
source: However, within families the median length of TEs that do not overlap H3K9me3 is highly similar to that of TEs that do (Pearson correlation for median TE lengths across families = 0.99; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), again suggesting that this is not a feature of length itself.
evidence: This is a direct result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is only a weak correlation between TE copy number and the proportion that overlap with H3K9me3 regions (Pearson's correlation = −0.47).
source: Across TE families, we found only a weak correlation between TE copy number and the proportion that overlap with H3K9me3 regions (Pearson's correlation = −0.47; permutation p=0.15; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TEs in the two smallest families (780 SVAs and 7,983 ERVKs) overlap H3K9me3 regions most often.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the general trend, TEs in the two smallest families (780 SVAs and 7,983 ERVKs) overlap H3K9me3 regions most often (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: After filtering lowly expressed genes, species emerges as the primary driver of variation in the RNA-seq data.
source: Indeed, after filtering lowly expressed genes, species emerges as the primary driver of variation in the RNA-seq data, as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RNA-seq data clusters primarily by species, and then by population.
source: After restricting the data to a set of human-chimpanzee orthologous exons (Blekhman et al., 2010) the RNA-seq data clusters primarily by species, and then by population (i.e. Caucasian or Yoruba/cell type of origin; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The observation of no association of inter-species expression divergence and TE silencing is robust with respect to a wide range of statistical cutoffs.
source: Again, we could only find a relationship between silencing and expression divergence when considering H3K9me3 overlapping TEs within 1 kb upstream of the TSS. The observation of no association of inter-species expression divergence and TE silencing is robust with respect to a wide range of statistical cutoffs used to classify either differential expression or differential silencing (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B and Table 9 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B and Table 9.

claim: The correlation between inter-species effect sizes for gene expression divergence and H3K9me3 enrichment increases to −0.14 when considering a 1 kb window upstream of the TSS.
source: Indeed, when we considered the entire distribution, the correlation between inter-species effect sizes for gene expression divergence and H3K9me3 enrichment is weak (Pearson's correlation = −0.0005 in a 10 kb window; the correlation in divergence increases somewhat to −0.14 when considering a 1 kb window upstream of the TSS; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from correlation analysis.

claim: Nearly as many genes show expression divergence consistent with the observed patterns of TE silencing divergence as those that show the opposite, inconsistent pattern.
source: Moreover, we observed nearly as many genes whose expression divergence is consistent with the observed patterns of TE silencing divergence (namely, TE silencing associated with lower expression level) as those that show the opposite, inconsistent pattern (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There is a relationship between expression divergence and silencing of TEs that overlap the promoter-associated mark but not of TEs that overlap enhancers.
source: We found a relationship between expression divergence and silencing of TEs that overlap the promoter-associated mark but not of TEs that overlap enhancers (typically further from the TSS; Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: 11 poly-adenylated TE types are expressed in chimpanzee.
source: Using our RNA-seq data, we identified 11 poly-adenylated TE types that are expressed in chimpanzee, and 7 that are expressed in human (Materials and methods; Table 10A in Supplementary file 1; note that this approach does not allow us to capture non-polyadenylated transcripts such as eRNAs).
evidence: This is a direct result from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 7 poly-adenylated TE types are expressed in human.
source: Using our RNA-seq data, we identified 11 poly-adenylated TE types that are expressed in chimpanzee, and 7 that are expressed in human (Materials and methods; Table 10A in Supplementary file 1; note that this approach does not allow us to capture non-polyadenylated transcripts such as eRNAs).
evidence: This is a direct result from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: HERVH elements are expressed in both human and chimpanzee.
source: In both species, we identified the expression of HERVH elements, which are known to be expressed in human pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Of the nine TE types that are annotated in both species and expressed in at least one species, 1,025 instances are contained within the orthologous TE set.
source: Of the nine TE types that are annotated in both species and expressed in at least one species, 1,025 instances are contained within our orthologous TE set (Table 10B in Supplementary file 1 and 123 instances overlap an H3K9me3 region.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expressed TEs.

claim: 123 instances of expressed TEs overlap an H3K9me3 region.
source: Of the nine TE types that are annotated in both species and expressed in at least one species, 1,025 instances are contained within our orthologous TE set (Table 10B in Supplementary file 1 and 123 instances overlap an H3K9me3 region.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expressed TEs.

claim: Only 14 of the expressed TE instances are enriched for H3K9me3 in human, and 22 in chimpanzee.
source: Only 14 of these TE instances are enriched for H3K9me3 in human, and 22 in chimpanzee (FDR < 0.01).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis of expressed TEs.

claim: Expressed TEs are proximal (within 10 kb) of only 19 orthologous genes.
source: These TEs are proximal (within 10 kb) of only 19 orthologous genes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expressed TEs and their proximity to genes.

claim: Gene regulation by an actively expressed poly-adenylated TE in one species is not a major mechanism of gene expression divergence.
source: In any case, even if there is such an association in these cases, the small number of instances suggests that gene regulation by an actively expressed poly-adenylated TE in one species is not a major mechanism of gene expression divergence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small number of expressed TEs associated with genes.

claim: There is no association between TE silencing and expression divergence when considering non-orthologous TEs.
source: We found, once again, that there is no association between TE silencing and expression divergence (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: A significant effect of non-orthologous TE silencing on gene expression divergence is only consistently observed when considering a 1 kb window immediately upstream of the TSS.
source: A significant effect is only consistently observed when considering a 1 kb window immediately upstream of the TSS (a set that includes 289 genes; Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: TE silencing by H3K9me3, regardless of orthology, has a modest effect on gene expression divergence in human and chimpanzee iPSC lines.
source: In other words, TE silencing by H3K9me3, regardless of orthology, has a modest effect on gene expression divergence in human and chimpanzee iPSC lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of both orthologous and non-orthologous TEs.

claim: 104 (41%) of 256 curated KRAB-ZNF genes overlap with orthologous H3K9me3 regions.
source: We found that 104 (41%) of these genes overlap with orthologous H3K9me3 regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 8A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of KRAB-ZNF gene overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: 78% of overlapping KRAB-ZNF genes (81 instances) have similar H3K9me3 enrichment in both species.
source: The proportion of KRAB-ZNFs with similar H3K9me3 enrichment in both species (78% of overlapping genes or 81 instances) is comparable to that observed for TEs (Figure 6—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of KRAB-ZNF gene H3K9me3 enrichment.

claim: 17 KRAB-ZNFs are enriched for H3K9me3 in human and 6 are enriched for H3K9me3 in chimpanzee.
source: 17 KRAB-ZNFs are enriched for H3K9me3 in human and 6 are enriched for H3K9me3 in chimpanzee.
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential enrichment analysis of KRAB-ZNF genes.

claim: 52% of KRAB-ZNF genes are classified as differentially expressed and 49% of all genes (FDR of 1%).
source: We found that the 256 KRAB-ZNF genes are no more likely to be differentially expressed between human and chimpanzee than all 17,354 genes (52% of KRAB-ZNFs are classified as differentially expressed and 49% of all genes; FDR of 1%; Figure 6—figure supplement 9A and Table 11 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: TEs preferentially silenced by H3K9me3 in chimpanzee are not associated more often with increased levels of H3K27me3 compared to TEs preferentially silenced by H3K9me3 in human.
source: We found that TEs preferentially silenced by H3K9me3 in chimpanzee are not associated more often with increased levels of H3K27me3 compared to TEs preferentially silenced by H3K9me3 in human (Figure 6—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 10.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are not redundant in silencing TEs across species.
source: This suggests that H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are not redundant in silencing TEs across species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of association between H3K27me3 and species-specific H3K9me3 silencing.

claim: H3K9me3 ChIP-seq reads are enriched at ZNF genes in both species.
source: As a first measure of quality of our data, consistent with previous reports, we observed an enrichment of H3K9me3 ChIP-seq reads at ZNF genes in both species (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)(Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Approximately 10% of the ChIP-seq data were excluded because peaks mapped outside orthologous genomic regions.
source: We excluded from our data peaks that mapped outside those orthologous genomic regions (approximately 10% of the ChIP-seq data were excluded; Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Table 3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the data filtering process.

claim: 160,113 orthologous ChIP-seq regions were defined.
source: We refer to this combined set as 160,113 orthologous ChIP-seq regions (rather than ChIP-seq peaks), because these regions are defined across all individuals, while the ChIP-seq peak may have been identified in only a subset of individuals.
evidence: This is a statement about the number of orthologous regions identified.

claim: 150,390 regions with at least one read count in more than half of the individuals were included in the analysis.
source: To avoid considering regions where we clearly have insufficient power to compare read counts across species, we included only the 150,390 regions with at least one read count in more than half of the individuals, regardless of species.
evidence: This is a statement about the data filtering process.

claim: One human individual was removed from subsequent analysis because it was an outlier.
source: As expected, data from different individuals cluster by species (with the exception of one human individual, which therefore was removed from subsequent analysis; Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10), and inter-species variation in read counts is somewhat greater than intra-species variation (Spearman's correlation in human vs. human = 0.90, chimpanzee vs. chimpanzee = 0.89, and human vs. chimpanzee = 0.80, Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is a statement about quality control and data filtering.
